name: GO Classes Test Series 2023 | Mixed Subjects | Full Length Test 2

question.text:
Imagine that you do not understand anything in this class. You would have to randomly guess the answer for the $5 \;\mathrm{MCQ}$ problems. Each $\mathrm{MCQ}$ has four options with an equal probability of each option being right. What is the probability that you can get at least two out of five right?

  1. $\displaystyle{} \sum_{k=2}^5\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^k$
     
  2. $\displaystyle{}\sum_{k=2}^5\left(\begin{array}{l}\begin{array}{l} 5 \\k \end{array}\end{array}\right)\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^k\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{5-k}$
     
  3. $\displaystyle{}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3$
     
  4. $\displaystyle{}\sum_{k=2}^5 \frac{5 !}{k !}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^k\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{5-k}$

Assume $\text{P(A)}=0.2, \text{P(B)}=0.6, \text{P(A} \cup \text{B})=0.5$. Then $\text{P[A|B]}=$

  1. $0.2$
  2. $0.3$
  3. $0.6$
  4. $0.5$

Consider the statement form $\mathrm{S}:$
$$
p \vee(\sim p \wedge q) \Rightarrow \sim q .
$$
Which of the following is true?

  1. $\text{S}$ is a tautology
  2. $\text{S}$ is a Contradiction
  3. $\text{S}$ is a Contingency
  4. Antecedent of $\text{S}$ is equivalent to consequent of $\text{S}$

The instructor in a probability course has a fair die and a fair coin and performs the following experiment: First the die is rolled and if the number on the die is $k$, the instructor then flips the coin $k$ times.
What is the probability that all the flips are heads?
  1. $32 / 63$
  2. $63 / 384$
  3. $1 / 3$
  4. None of these

The power set $\mathcal{P}((\text{A} \times \text{B}) \cup(B \times \text{A}))$ has the same number of elements as the power set $\mathcal{P}((\text{A} \times \text{B}) \cup(\text{A} \times \text{B}))$ if and only if

  1. $\text{A = B}$
  2. $\text{A}=\emptyset$ or $\text{B}=\emptyset$
  3. $\text{B}=\emptyset$ or $\text{A = B}$
  4. $\text{A} = \emptyset$ or $\text{B} = \emptyset$ or $\text{A = B}$
Let $\mathrm{G}$ be a non-cyclic group of order $57 .$ Then the number of elements of order $5$ in $\mathrm{G}$ is _______

Let $n \in \mathrm{N}$,

Consider the following two combinatorial identities :

  1. $\left(\begin{array}{c}2 n \\2\\\end{array}\right)=2\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\2\\\end{array}\right)+n^2 .$
  2. $\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\0\\\end{array}\right)+2^1\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\1\\\end{array}\right)+2^2\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\2\\\end{array}\right)+\ldots+2^k\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\k\\\end{array}\right)+\ldots+2^n\left(\begin{array}{l}n\\n\\\end{array}\right)=3^n .$

Which of the above are correct?

  1. Only $1$
  2. Only $2$
  3. Both
  4. None

A full binary tree is a rooted tree in which every internal node has exactly two children. How many internal nodes are there in a full binary tree with $500$ leaves?

  1. $250$
  2. $499$
  3. $500$
  4. $501$
The number of different Total order relations on a set of $7$ elements is _______

Let us consider a die with six faces, each face with a value in $\{1,2,3,4$, $5,6\}$. Roll the die four consecutive times and write down the sequence of the numbers that show up. How many sequences have " $3$ " in at least two of these four rolls and no "$5$" in any roll.
What is the order of smallest non-cyclic group?

Let $f$ be a function from a set $\text{X}$ to a set $\text{Y}$. Consider the following statements.

  • $\text{P} :$ For each $x \in \text{X}$, there exists $y \in \text{Y}$ such that $f(x)=y$.
  • $\text{Q} :$ For each $y \in \text{Y}$, there exists $x \in \text{X}$ such that $f(x)=y$.
  • $\text{R} :$ There exist $x_1, x_2 \in \text{X}$ such that $x_1 \neq x_2$ and $f\left(x_1\right)=f\left(x_2\right)$.

The negation of the statement " $f$ is one-to-one and onto $\text{Y}$ " is

  1. $\text{P}$ or not $\text{R}$
  2. $\text{R}$ or not $\text{P}$
  3. $\text{R}$ or not $\text{Q}$
  4. $\text{P}$ and not $\text{R}$

Consider the two statements below.

  • $\text{S1:}$ Disjoint events are independent.
  • $\text{S2:}$ If events $\text{A}$ and $\text{B}$ are independent, then conditioned on any other event $\text{C, A}$ and $\text{B}$ are still independent.

Which of the following option is correct?

  1. $\text{S1}$ is correct but $\mathrm{S} 2$ is incorrect
  2. $\mathrm{S} 1$ is incorrect but $\mathrm{S} 2$ is correct
  3. Both are true
  4. Both are False

A graph is said to be $2$-colourable if each vertex can be coloured either red or blue and no two vertices of the same colour are connected by an edge. If some graph is not $2$-colorable, then we can reduce it to become $2$-colorable by deleting some edges. We are given any simple graph with $101$ nodes. $k$ is the least required number of edges we have to delete in order to make this graph $2$-colorable (Eg: $k=0$ for a graph which is already $2$-colorable).
The minimum value for ' $k$ ' to reach the worst case is _______

Let $\text{A}$ be any set.
The following are the definitions of Irreflexive and Asymmetric Relations :

  1. A binary relation $\text{R}$ on a set $\mathcal{A}$ is irreflexive iff $(x, x) \notin \text{R}$ for all $x \in \mathcal{A}$.
  2. A binary relation $\text{R}$ on a set $\mathcal{A}$ is asymmetric iff whenever $(x, y) \in \text{R}$, then $(y, x) \notin \text{R}$.

We define a "strict order relation" as follows :
A binary relation $\text{R}$ on a set $\text{A}$ is a strict order on $\text{A}$ iff $\text{R}$ is irreflexive and transitive.
Which of the following is/are true?

  1. Every strict order is asymmetric.
  2. Every strict order is total order relation.
  3. Every strict order is antisymmetric.
  4. Every relation which is both Irreflexive and Asymmetric, is strict order.

Which of the following is NOT an eigenvector of the matrix $A=\left[\begin{array}{lcr}2 & 3 & -1 \\
0 & 1 & 2 \\ 
0 & 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right] ?$

  1. $\left[\begin{array}{c}4\\
    -3\\
    3\\ \end{array}\right]$
  2. $\star\left[\begin{array}{l}2 \\
    0 \\
    1\\ \end{array}\right]$
  3. $\left[\begin{array}{l}1\\
    0\\
    0\\ \end{array}\right]$
  4. All of the others answers are eigenvectors of $\text{A}.$

Let $\text{Y}$ be a Normal random variable with mean $3$ and variance $4.$

What is $\mathbf{P}(2<Y<4)?$ 

It is given that $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{Z}<0.5)=0.6915$ for standard normal random variable $\mathrm{Z}$. (Answer upto $2$ decimals)

  1. $0.38$
  2. $0.48$
  3. $0.69$
  4. $0.50$

Suppose there are ten balls in an urn, four blue, four red, and two green. The balls are also numbered $1$ to $10 .$ How many ways are there to select an ordered sample of four balls without replacement such that the number $\text{B} \geq 0$ of blue balls, the number $\mathrm{R} \geq 0$ of red balls, and the number $\mathrm{G} \geq 0$ of green balls are all different?

Consider a $5 \times 6$ rectangular grid as depicted in Figure $1.$ A staircase walk is a path in the grid which moves only right or up.

What is the total number of staircase walks from $\text{A}$ to $\text{B}$ that may or may not pass through the point $\text{P?}$
The number of partitions of the set $\text{X} = \{a, b, c, d\}$ with “$a$” and “$b$” in the same block is ________

Assume $v$ is an eigenvector to $\text{A}$ with eigenvalue 3 and $\text{A}$ is invertible. Consider below set of statements.
$$
\begin{array}{|l|}
\hline \qquad \textbf{Statements}\\
\hline \text{A}^5 \text{ has an eigenvalue } 3^5\\
\hline \text{A}^{-1} \text{ has an eigenvalue } 1 / 3\\
\hline \text{A}^\text{T} \text{ has an eigenvalue } 1 / 3\\
\hline \text{A}^5 \text{ has an eigenvector } v\\
\hline \text{A}^{-1} \text{ has an eigenvector } v\\
\hline \text{A}^\text{T} \text{ has an eigenvector } v\\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
How many statements are true out of all?

  1. $3$
  2. $4$
  3. $5$
  4. $6$

Let $\text{Z}$ be a random variable with pmf $p_\text{Z}(k)=\frac{c}{\left(2^k\right)}$ for $k \in\{1,2,3,4\}$ and zero else. Determine the value of the mean $\text{E[Z]}.$
  1. $\frac{15}{16}$
  2. $\frac{26}{15}$
  3. $\frac{13}{8}$
  4. $\frac{64}{15}$

A parallel system functions whenever at least one of its components works. Consider a parallel system of $n$ components and suppose that each component works with probability $p$ independently.
What is the probability the system is functioning?

  1. $(1-p)^n$
  2. $p^n$
  3. $1-(1-p)^n$
  4. $1-p^n$

Let $\text{A}$ be a $3 \times 3$ matrix with rows $\mathbf{R}_1, \mathbf{R}_2$ and $\mathbf{R}_3$. Suppose the following row operations bring $\text{A}$ to the identity matrix:
$$
\text{A} \stackrel{\text{R}_1 \leftrightarrow \text{R}_2}{\longrightarrow} \text{A}_1 \stackrel{\text{R}_3 \rightarrow \frac{1}{5} \text{R}_3}{\longrightarrow} \text{A}_2 \stackrel{\text{R}_3 \rightarrow \text{R}_3 + 2 \text{R}_1}{\longrightarrow} \text{I}_3
$$
where $\text{I}_3$ is the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix. Then,

  1. $\operatorname{det} \text{A}=5$
  2. $\operatorname{det} \text{A}=-5$
  3. $\operatorname{det} \text{A}=-\frac{1}{5}$
  4. $\operatorname{det} \text{A}=\frac{1}{5}$

Which of the following statements is true for every matrix $\text{M}$ with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, where $m<n?$

  1. The system $\text{M} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has no solution.
  2. The system $\text{M} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has infinitely many solutions.
  3. For every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$, the system $\text{M} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has infinitely many solutions.
  4. For some $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$, the system $\text{M} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has a unique solution.

We call a couple a soulmate couple if both of them have each other as the first person on their preference lists. If there are $n$ men and $n$ women, and all of their preference lists are independently uniformly generated over all permutations, what is the expected number of soulmate couples?
  1. $n$
  2. $1 / n$
  3. $1$
  4. $2 n$

An Euler circuit of an undirected graph is a circuit in which each edge of the graph appears exactly once. Which of the following undirected graphs must have an Euler circuit?

  1. A complete graph with $12$ vertices
  2. A complete graph with $13$ vertices
  3. A tree with $13$ vertices
  1. I only
  2. II only
  3. III only
  4. I and II Only

In this problem, we will consider a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$.
The entry of $A$ in the position $(i, j)$ is denoted by $\text{A}_{i, j}$, and it is distributed as follows:
$$
\text{A}_{i, j}=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
0 & \text { with probability } & 0.5\\
1 & \text { with probability } & 0.25\\
-1 & \text { with probability } & 0.25\\
\end{array}\right.
$$
What is the expected number of non-zero elements in the matrix $\text{A}.$

  1. $n^ 2 / 2 $
  2. $n^ 2 / 4 $
  3. $n^ 2 $
  4. $n$

Let $\text{A}$ be an $n \times n$-matrix and let $\text{B}$ be an $m \times n$-matrix. Consider the following statements.

  • $\text{(S1)}$ If $\text{B}$ has orthonormal columns, then $\text{B}^\text{T}$ has orthonormal columns.
  • $\text{(S2)}$ If $\text{A}^\text{T}$ is an orthogonal matrix, then $\text{A}$ is an orthogonal matrix.

Which of the two statements are always true?

  1. Neither $\text{(S1)}$ nor $\text{(S2)}.$
  2. Only $\text{(S1)}.$
  3. Both $\text{(S1)}$ and $\text{(S2)}.$
  4. Only $\text{(S2)}.$

A carton contains $4$ red and $6$ green apples. Two apples are drawn at random without replacement, and their color is noted. Determine the probability that at least one of the apples drawn is green.
  1. $2 / 3$
  2. $13 / 15$
  3. $5 / 7$
  4. $6 / 7$

Suppose $\text{Z}_1, \text{Z}_2, \text{Z}_3$ are independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
The random variable is defined as follows:
$$
\text{S}= \begin{cases}\text{Z}_2 \text{Z}_3 & \text { if } \text{Z}_1=1,\\
\text{Z}_2+\text{Z}_3 & \text { if } \text{Z}_1=0 .\end{cases}
$$
Find $\text{P(S}=1)$.

  1. $3 / 8$
  2. $1 / 2$
  3. $1 / 8$
  4. None of these
Suppose a test is $99 \%$ accurate and $1 \%$ of people have a disease. What is the probability that you have the disease given that you tested positive?

Given a graph $\mathrm{G}$ is a connected planar simple graph with ' $e$ ' edges and ' $v$ ' vertices, with $v \geq 3$ and if all cycles in $\text{G}$ have length $\geq 4$, then which of the following relations hold always?
 

  1. $e \leq 2 v-4$
  2. $e \leq 2 v-2$
  3. $e \leq 3 v-4$
  4. None of these

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. For all sets $\text{A, B}, $ and $\text{C, A - (B - C) = (A - B) - C}$.
  2. For all sets $\text{A, B}, $ and $\text{C, (A - B)} \cap \text{(C - B) = (A} \cap \text{C)- B}$.
  3. For all sets $\text{A, B}, $ and $\text{C, (A - B)} \cap \text{(C - B) = A - (B} \cup \text{C)}$.
  4. For all sets $\text{A, B}, $ and $\text{C},$ if $\text{A} \cap \text{C = B} \cap \text{C}$ then $\text{A = B}$.

For a connected, undirected graph $\text{G = (V, E)},$ which of the following must be true?

  1. $\sum_{v \in \text{V}}$ degree $(\mathrm{v})$ is even.
  2. $|\mathrm{E}| \geq|\mathrm{V}|-1$
  3. $\mathrm{G}$ has at least one vertex with degree $1.$
  1. I only
  2. I, II only
  3. I, III only
  4. I, II, III

Let $f:\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\} \rightarrow\{a, b, c, d, e\}$. In one-line notation, $f=(e, a, b, b, a, c, c, a, c)$ (use number order on the domain). Which is correct?

  1. $\operatorname{Image}(f)=\{a, b, c, d, e\}, \operatorname{Coimage} (f)=\{\{6,7,9\},\{2,5,8\},\{3,4\},\{1\}\}$
  2. $\operatorname{Image}(f)=\{a, b, c, e\}, \operatorname{Coimage}(f)=\{\{6,7,9\},\{2,5,8\},\{3,4\}\}$
  3. $\operatorname{Image}(f)=\{a, b, c, e\}, \operatorname{Coimage} (f)=\{\{6,7,9\},\{2,5,8\},\{3,4\},\{1\}\}$
  4. $\operatorname{Image}(f)=\{a, b, c, e\}, \operatorname{Coimage}(f)=\{\{6,7,9,2,5,8\},\{3,4\},\{1\}\}$

Number of Linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to the matrix
$$
\left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
-2 & 2 & -1 \\
4 & 0 & 3 \\
\end{array}\right)
$$

Let $f: \text{X} \rightarrow \text{Y}$ and $g: \text{Y} \rightarrow \text{Z}.$ Let $h=g \circ f: \text{X} \rightarrow \text{Z}.$ Suppose $g$ is one-to-one and onto. Which of the following is FALSE?

  1. If $f$ is one-to-one then $h$ is one-to-one and onto.
  2. If $f$ is not onto then $h$ is not onto.
  3. If $f$ is not one-to-one then $h$ is not one-to-one.
  4. If $f$ is one-to-one then $h$ is one-to-one.

Which of the following statements are true for an $n \times n$ matrix $\text{M}?$

  1. $\operatorname{det} \text{M} = \operatorname{det} \text{M}^\text{T}.$
  2. The equation $\text{M} \vec{x}=\overrightarrow{0}$ always has a solution.
  3. $\text{M}$ is invertible if and only if zero is not an eigenvalue of $\text{M}.$
  4. $\text{M}$ has at most $n$ eigenvalues.

In a group $\mathrm{G},$ every element other than the identity element has order $2$ then $\mathrm{G}$ is?
  1. Abelian group
  2. Cyclic group
  3. Non-abelian group
  4. Non-cyclic group

Which of the following propositional logic formulas is/are valid?

  1. $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge \neg q \rightarrow \neg p$
  2. $(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow(p \rightarrow \neg q)$
  3. $(p \vee q \rightarrow \mathrm{r}) \vee p \vee q$
  4. $(p \vee q) \wedge(p \rightarrow r \wedge q) \wedge(q \rightarrow \neg r \wedge p)$

Let $\text{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}
1 & -1 \\
0 & 2
\end{array}\right]$, and let $\text{B}$ be a $2 \times 3$ matrix. Suppose that the second row of $\text{(A B)}^\text{T}$ is $\mathbf{v}=[-1 \quad 3]$
Compute the second column of $\text{B}$.

  1. $
    \left[\begin{array}{c}
    -1\\
    3\\
    \end{array}\right]
    $
  2. $
    \left[\begin{array}{l}
    \frac{1}{2}\\
    \frac{3}{2}\\
    \end{array}\right]
    $
  3. $
    \left[\begin{array}{l}
    \frac{1}{3}\\
    1\\
    \end{array}\right]
    $
  4. $
    \left[\begin{array}{c}
    3\\
    -1\\
    \end{array}\right]
    $
Find the number of positive integers $n \in N$, such that $1 \leq n \leq 1000$, which are not divisible by either $4,10$ or $15 .$

Consider a biased coin with $\text{P(H)}=0.6$. Suppose we repeatedly toss untill we get exactly $3$ heads.
What is the probability that you have to flip it exactly $8$ times to see exactly $3$ heads? (Hint: The last flip must be heads, but the other two heads can come anywhere in the previous $7$ flips)

  1. $
    \left(\begin{array}{l}
    7\\
    2\\
    \end{array}\right)(0.6)^2(0.4)^5
    $
  2. $
    0.6 *\left(\begin{array}{l}
    7\\
    2\\
    \end{array}\right)(0.6)^2(0.4)^5
    $
  3. $
    \left(\begin{array}{l}
    8\\
    3\\
    \end{array}\right)(0.6)^3(0.4)^5
    $
  4. $
    0.6 *\left(\begin{array}{l}
    8\\
    2\\
    \end{array}\right)(0.6)^2(0.4)^5
    $

Suppose that the characteristic polynomial of an arbitrary matrix $\text{A}$ is
$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)^2 .
$$
Which of the following can you determine from this information?

  1. The trace of $\text{A}.$
  2. The determinant of $\text{A}.$
  3. The exact rank of $\text{A}$ (not an upper or lower bound).
  4. The eigenvalues of $\text{A}.$

Let $\text{A}$ be a $10 \times 8$ matrix and $\mathbf{b}$ be a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{10}$ such that the equation $\text{A} \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has a unique solution. Which of the following statements cannot be correct?
  1. $\operatorname{rank} \text{A}=10$.
  2. The columns of $\text{A}$ are linearly independent.
  3. Every row of $\text{A}$ contains a pivot position.
  4. Nullity of $\text{A}$ is $2.$

Roll a $(6$-sided) die. Let $\text{A}$ be the event that the outcome on the die is an odd number. Let $\text{B}$ be the event that the outcome on the die is $3$ or smaller. Let $\mathrm{C}$ be the event that the outcome on the die is $4$ or smaller.
Which of the following is/are true?
  1. $\text{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ are independent
  2. $\text{B}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ are independent
  3. $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ are independent
  4. $\text{A, B}$ and $\text{C}$ are independent

Suppose $\text{Y}$ has a discrete distribution with pmf given by
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline y & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\
\hline p_\textsf{Y}(y) & 1 / 2 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 8 & 1 / 8\\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Calculate $\text{E}\left[(\text{Y}-1)^2\right]?$

  1. $1 / 4$
  2. $1 / 8$
  3. $9 / 8$
  4. $3 / 4$

If $\text{F}(x)=f(g(x))$, where $f(-2)=8, f^{\prime}(-2)=4, f^{\prime}(5)=3, g(5)=-2, g^{\prime}(5)=6,$ find $\text{F}^{\prime}(5).$
  1. $24$
  2. $8$
  3. $12$
  4. $20$

Which of the following associative multiplication tables defined on the set $\mathrm{G}=\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}\}$ form a group?

  1. $\begin{array}{c|cccc}
    \circ & a & b & c & d\\
    \hline a & a & c & d & a\\
    b & b & b & c & d\\
    c & c & d & a & b\\
    d & d & a & b & c\\
    \end{array}$

  2. $\begin{array}{c|cccc}
    \circ & a & b & c & d \\
    \hline a & a & b & c & d \\
    b & b & c & d & a \\
    c & c & d & a & b \\
    d & d & a & b & c \\
    \end{array}$

  3. $\begin{array}{c|cccc}
    \circ & a & b & c & d \\
    \hline a & a & b & c & d \\
    b & b & a & d & c \\
    c & c & d & a & b \\
    d & d & c & b & a \\
    \end{array}$

  4. $
    \begin{array}{c|cccc}
    \circ & a & b & c & d \\
    \hline a & a & b & c & d \\
    b & b & a & c & d \\
    c & c & b & a & d \\
    d & d & d & b & c \\
    \end{array}
    $

Which of the following is true in the context of propositional logic?
  1. There is some statement $p \Rightarrow q$ that is not equivalent to its contrapositive.
  2. There is some statement $p \Rightarrow q$ that is not equivalent to its converse.
  3. There is some statement $p \Rightarrow q$ that is equivalent to its converse.
  4. There is some statement $p \Rightarrow q$ such that converse of $p \Rightarrow q$ is not equivalent to inverse of $p \Rightarrow q$.

To show that the circuit corresponding to the Boolean expression $(\text{P} \wedge \text{Q}) \vee(\sim P \wedge \text{Q}) \vee$ $(\sim \text{P}\wedge \sim \text{Q})$ can be represented using two logical gates, one shows that this Boolean expression is equal to $\sim \text{P}\vee \text{Q}$. The circuit corresponding to $(\text{P} \wedge \text{Q} \wedge \text{R}) \vee(\sim \text{P}\wedge \text{Q} \wedge$ $\text{R}) \vee(\sim \text{P}\wedge(\sim \text{Q} \vee \sim \text{R})$ computes the same function as the circuit corresponding to

  1. $(\text{P} \wedge \text{Q}) \vee \sim \text{R}$
  2. $\text{P} \vee(\text{Q} \wedge \text{R})$
  3. $\sim \text{P}\vee(\text{Q} \wedge \text{R})$
  4. $(\text{P} \wedge \sim \text{Q}) \vee \text{R}$
The number of subgroups of a cyclic group of order $12$ is ______

Let $\text{A}$ be a $3 \times 3$ matrix with characteristic equation $-\lambda^3-\lambda^2+2 \lambda=0$. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\text{A}$ is invertible.
  2. $\lambda=-2$ is an eigenvalue of $\text{A}.$
  3. $\lambda=1$ is an eigenvalue of $\text{A}$ with multiplicity $2 .$
  4. The eigenvalues of $\text{A}^2$ are $0,1 ,$ and $4 .$

Consider the set $\mathrm{G}=\{\mathrm{e}, \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d}, \mathrm{f}\}$ with operation $\ast$ defined by the table below. $\left(\mathrm{G},\ast\right)$ is a group.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \ast & e & a & b & c & d & f\\
\hline e & e & a & b & c & d & f\\
\hline a & a & b & e & d & f & c\\
\hline b & b & e & a & f & c & d\\
\hline c & c & f & d & e & b & a\\
\hline d & d & c & f & a & e & b\\
\hline f & f & d & c & b & a & e\\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Which of the following is False?

  1. It is abelian.
  2. Order of "$a$" is $6 .$
  3. It is a cyclic group.
  4. Number of elements of order $2$ is $3.$

There are $5$ accidents/month on a highway. Accidents on this highway are distributed as a Poisson random variable. Find the probability there will be no accidents in a given year.
  1. $1-e^{-60}$
  2. $e^{-60}$
  3. $1-e^{-5}$
  4. $e^{-5}$

  2. $2^{|\text{A}|} \geq|\text{B}|$

What is $\operatorname{det}\left(2 \text{C}^3 \text{BA}\left(\text{C}^\text{T}\right)^{-3}\right)\;$_________

Let $\text{A}$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Consider the following two statements:

  • $\text{(U1)}$ The matrix $3 \text{A}$ has the same eigenvectors as $\text{A}$.
  • $\text{(U2)}$ The matrix $3 \text{A}$ has the same eigenvalues as $\text{A}$.

Which of the two statements are always true?

  1. Only Statement $\text{(U1)}$ is correct.
  2. Statement $\text{(U1)}$ and Statement $\text{(U2)}$ are correct.
  3. Neither Statement $\text{(U1)}$ nor Statement $\text{(U2)}$ is correct.
  4. Only Statement $\text{(U2)}$ is correct.

Let $\text{A}$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Its only eigenvalues are $1,2,3,4,5$, possibly with multiplicities.

What is the nullity of the matrix $\text{A + I}_n,$ where $\text{I}_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix?

  1. $0$
  2. $1$
  3. $n-1$
  4. $n-5$

Which of the following statements is/are True?

  1. $\{2,3,4\} \subseteq \text{A}$ implies that $2 \in \text{A}$ and $\{3,4\} \subseteq \text{A}.$
  2. $\{2,3,4\} \in \text{A}$ and $\{2,3\} \in \text{B}$ implies that $\{4\} \subseteq \text{A - B}.$
  3. $\text{A} \cap \text{B} \supseteq\{2,3,4\}$ implies that $\{2,3,4\} \subseteq \text{A}$ and $\{2,3,4\} \subseteq \text{B}.$
  4. $\text{A - B} \supseteq\{3,4\}$ and $\{1,2\} \subseteq \text{B}$ implies that $\{1,2,3,4\} \subseteq \text{A} \cup \text{B}.$

Suppose $\text{A}$ is an $8 \times 12$ matrix and $\vec{b}$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^8$ such that the equation $\text{A} \vec{x}=\vec{b}$ is inconsistent.
Which of the following option is/are TRUE ?

  1. rank $\text{A} = 8.$
  2. $\operatorname{rank}(\text{A})+\operatorname{Nullity}(\text{A})=12$.
  3. The homogeneous equation $\text{A} \vec{x}=\overrightarrow{0}$ is inconsistent.
  4. At least one row of $\text{A}$ does not contain a pivot position.

A $k$-ary tree is a tree in which every node has at most $k$ children. In a $k$-ary tree with $n$ nodes and height $h,$ which of the following is an upper bound for the maximum number of leaves as a function of $h, k$, and $n?$ (height of the tree is the number of edges in the longest path from root to some leaf)

  1. $\log_k n$
  2. $n / \log _{k}(n)$
  3. $k^h$
  4. $h^k$

Which of the following formulas is a formalization of the sentence: "Every connected and circuit-free graph is a tree". Where cir( $\mathrm{x})$ means " $\mathrm{x}$ has circuit"

  1. $\forall \mathrm{x}[(\operatorname{conn}(\mathrm{x}) \wedge \neg \operatorname{cir}(\mathrm{x})) \rightarrow \operatorname{tree}(\mathrm{x})]$
  2. $\neg \exists x[(\operatorname{conn}(\mathrm{x}) \wedge \neg \operatorname{cir}(\mathrm{x})) \wedge \neg \operatorname{tree}(\mathrm{x})]$
  3. $\forall \mathrm{x}[(\operatorname{conn}(\mathrm{x}) \wedge \neg \operatorname{cir}(\mathrm{x})) \wedge \operatorname{tree}(\mathrm{x})]$
  4. $\forall \mathrm{x}[(\operatorname{conn}(\mathrm{x}) \wedge \operatorname{cir}(\mathrm{x})) \rightarrow \operatorname{tree}(\mathrm{x})]$
